explanations.explanation: The altar is the target. Jeroboam, king of Israel, is standing beside it to burn incense when the man of God calls out, "O altar, O altar, this is what the LORD says…" (1 Kings 13:2). The message is aimed at the altar, and the king is right beside it.

Jeroboam is a king, so the throne is a fair guess, friend. But the text puts him standing beside the altar, and that's what the man of God cries out against. The throne never comes up in this scene. The altar gets the whole message.

A gate would make for a dramatic speech, but no gate shows up in this scene. Jeroboam is standing beside his altar, and the man of God cries out against that altar. Next time, look for where the king is standing.

That's the sign. The man of God says, “Surely the altar will be split apart, and the ashes upon it will be poured out.” A sign is something you can check with your own eyes. Jeroboam doesn't have to take anybody's word for it.
The golden calf is real. Jeroboam set one up in Bethel (1 Kings 12:29). But this sign says nothing about it melting. The sign is about the altar and the ashes on it.
That would be some sign, but it isn't this one. The man of God says the sign is about the altar and the ashes sitting on it. The sky doesn't come up in his sign at all.

Jeroboam stretches out his hand and says, “Seize him!” But the hand he stretched out "…withered, so that he could not pull it back." He orders a man seized and can't even take his own hand back. I think that's a long moment to stand there holding a pose you didn't choose.

White as snow is a picture from another story (Exodus 4:6), not this one. Here the text says the hand withered, and the king could not pull it back. Keep your eyes on the verse, baker, and the hand tells you what happened.
A shaking hand is a fair guess, but that's not what the text says. The hand withers, and the king can't pull it back. It stays stretched out toward the man of God.

Jeroboam says, “Intercede with the LORD your God and pray for me that my hand may be restored.” The man he wanted seized is now the man he's asking for help. The text gives us what the king asks, and it doesn't say what was going on inside him.
Jeroboam was standing beside that altar to burn incense, so I see the guess. But the king doesn't ask for a sacrifice. He asks the man of God to intercede with the LORD and pray for him.
Fasting means going without food, and that isn't what Jeroboam asks for. He says, “Intercede with the LORD your God and pray for me…” Praying is the request, and the man of God answers it.

The king's offer sounds generous, and the text says it plainly: come home, refresh yourself, and I'll give you a reward. But the man of God doesn't accept. He says, “If you were to give me half your possessions, I still would not go with you…” True would have been a reasonable guess, but the answer is no.

He turns the offer down flat. The text has him say, “If you were to give me half your possessions, I still would not go with you, nor would I eat bread or drink water in this place.” A king's reward and a seat at his table, and the answer is no. Even Papa would have to think twice about that one.

explanations.answer: The LORD commanded him not to
explanations.explanation: The man of God says it himself: “For this is what I was commanded by the word of the LORD: ‘You must not eat bread or drink water or return by the way you came.’…” It's a command from the LORD. That's why a king's reward can't move him.

explanations.answer: He doesn't trust the king's food
explanations.explanation: That's a sensible guess, but the text never says he distrusts the food. The reason he gives is that the LORD commanded it. The command covers bread, water and the way home.

explanations.answer: He wants to get home before dark
explanations.explanation: Getting home before dark would be a fine reason for a hurry, but the text never mentions the time of day. The man of God points to the word of the LORD: “You must not eat bread or drink water or return by the way you came.” The command is his reason.

That's it. The text says he "…went another way and did not return by the way he had come to Bethel." The command had three parts, and he follows the road part as well. So far he's sticking to every piece of it.

explanations.answer: He goes back the way he came
explanations.explanation: The command he quotes includes not returning by the way he came, so that's the one road he avoids. The text says he "…went another way…" He leaves Bethel on a different road.

explanations.answer: He waits for the king's escort
explanations.explanation: No escort is mentioned. The king does invite him home and offers a reward, but the man of God turns that down. The text says he went another way and did not return by the way he had come.

The old prophet asks his sons, “Which way did he go?” and they show him the road the man of God took. Short question, friend, but watch what it sets in motion. Next thing you know, he's telling his sons to saddle the donkey (1 Kings 13:12, 13). I think somebody just made up his mind.
The sons tell their father what the man did and what he said to the king. But the question the old prophet asks is a short one: “Which way did he go?” The king's mood isn't part of it.
His sons have already told him the deeds and the words of the man of God. The old prophet's question is about the road: “Which way did he go?” His looks never come up.
Bread sounds nice, so I see the guess. But the man of God answers, “I cannot go home with you, and I will not eat bread or drink water with you in this place.” His answer is no.

The man of God says no. He answers, “I cannot go home with you, and I will not eat bread or drink water with you in this place.” Then he explains that the LORD told him, “You must not eat bread or drink water there or return by the way you came.” So the old prophet's invitation gets turned down.

The text says so outright: "The old prophet was lying to him…" He says, “I too am a prophet like you, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD…” but the man of God had already been told something different by the word of the LORD. We're told this plainly so we know the angel claim wasn't true.

The text doesn't leave this one open. It says, "The old prophet was lying to him…" The old prophet claims an angel spoke to him by the word of the LORD, and the text calls that a lie. So that claim can't be trusted.

explanations.answer: Goes back and eats at his house
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says: the man of God "…went back with him, ate bread in his house, and drank water." He had told the king and then the old prophet he wouldn't. Now he does the very thing he said he wouldn't do.
That's what his earlier words would lead you to expect, so I get the guess. But the text says he went back with the old prophet. He ate bread and drank water in his house.

explanations.answer: Asks the LORD to confirm it first
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text shows him asking. It says he went back with the old prophet, ate bread in his house, and drank water. Asking would have been a different story, and that's not the one we're given.
The text says, "…the word of the LORD came to the prophet who had brought him back…" It comes while they're sitting at the table. The old prophet is the one who tells the man of God what it says.
The text doesn't name Jeroboam anywhere in this scene. It says the word of the LORD came to the prophet who had brought him back. That's the old prophet, and he's the one who cries out the message.

His sons saddle the donkey earlier, but the text doesn't name them in this scene. It says the word of the LORD came to the prophet who had brought the man back. He's the one who cries out the message.

Here's the message: “Because you have defied the word of the LORD and have not kept the commandment that the LORD your God gave you…” Defied is a strong word, and the LORD chose it. It names what happened at that table.
Obeyed is the opposite of what the message says. The LORD says the man has defied His word and has not kept the commandment He gave. That's why the message turns serious.

Forgotten is an understandable guess, but it isn't the word in the text. The message says, “Because you have defied the word of the LORD and have not kept the commandment that the LORD your God gave you…” Defied is the word.

explanations.answer: Report it in the old prophet's city
explanations.explanation: That's what they do. The men passing by see the body and the lion beside it, and they go and report it in the city where the old prophet lived. The text doesn't say what they did beyond that.

explanations.answer: Bury the body by the roadside
explanations.explanation: The text never has the passersby bury him. They see the body and the lion, and then they go report it in the old prophet's city. The burying comes later, and the old prophet is the one who does it.

explanations.answer: Carry the body back to Judah
explanations.explanation: Nobody carries the body to Judah. The men passing by report what they saw in the city where the old prophet lived. The old prophet later brings the body to his own city.

I understand why chance might come to mind, but that isn't what the old prophet says. He says, “Therefore the LORD has delivered him to the lion, and it has mauled him and killed him, according to the word that the LORD had spoken to him.” He ties it to the word of the LORD, and chance never comes up. This is a heavy part of the story.

He doesn't call it chance. He says, “It is the man of God who disobeyed the command of the LORD.” Then he adds that the LORD has delivered him to the lion according to the word the LORD had spoken to him. It's a heavy moment, and the old prophet treats it that way.

The text says, "The lion had not eaten the body or mauled the donkey." The old prophet finds the body with the donkey and the lion standing beside it. I think that's a strange scene to ride up on, and the text lets it speak for itself.

The text says the opposite. It says, "The lion had not eaten the body or mauled the donkey." The old prophet finds the body lying in the road, with the donkey and the lion standing beside it. So neither the body nor the donkey has been eaten or mauled.

explanations.answer: Lays it in his own tomb
explanations.explanation: He lifts the body onto the donkey and brings it back to his own city to mourn and bury him. Then he lays it in his own tomb. Earlier the LORD's message said the man's body would never reach the tomb of his fathers (1 Kings 13:22). The text just tells us where he's laid.
The body doesn't go to Judah. The old prophet brings it back to his own city. There he lays it in his own tomb.
The altar was split apart, but the text never has the body taken there. The old prophet carries it to his own city. He lays it in his own tomb and they lament over him.

The old prophet tells his sons, “When I die, you must bury me in the tomb where the man of God is buried. Lay my bones beside his bones…” He's thinking ahead to his own burial. He gives his reason too: the message the man of God cried out against the altar “…will surely come to pass.”
A sword would make this a battle story, and this isn't one. The old prophet says, “Lay my bones beside his bones…” Bones are the word in his request.
A staff is a travel-ready kind of guess, but it isn't in the verse. The old prophet says, “Lay my bones beside his bones…” He asks that his own bones be laid beside the man of God's.

explanations.answer: The man's message will surely come true
explanations.explanation: The old prophet says it right after the burial: “…for the message that he cried out by the word of the LORD against the altar in Bethel and against all the shrines on the high places in the cities of Samaria will surely come to pass.” That's the reason the text gives. It names the message the man of God cried out.

explanations.answer: The man had asked to be buried with him
explanations.explanation: The man of God never asks for that. The text gives the old prophet's own reason: the message the man cried out will surely come to pass. That's the reason for lying beside him.

explanations.answer: The king had commanded it for prophets
explanations.explanation: Jeroboam's commands in this passage go the other way. First he says, “Seize him!” and later he makes anyone a priest for the high places. The old prophet gives his own reason, that the man's message will surely come to pass.

explanations.answer: Makes anyone who wants it a priest
explanations.explanation: That's the text: Jeroboam "…again he appointed priests for the high places from every class of people. He ordained anyone who desired to be a priest of the high places." The word again tells us he's done this before. After all that happened, he keeps going.

explanations.answer: Builds a brand new altar in Dan
explanations.explanation: Dan is a real place in the story. Jeroboam set up a golden calf there earlier, along with one in Bethel (1 Kings 12:29). But this passage doesn't mention a new altar in Dan. It says he appointed priests for the high places.

explanations.answer: Sets up a third golden calf
explanations.explanation: Two calves are named in the story: one in Bethel and one in Dan (1 Kings 12:29). A third isn't mentioned. In this passage Jeroboam appoints priests for the high places from every class of people.

The text says it plainly: “…this was the sin of the house of Jeroboam that led to its extermination and destruction from the face of the earth.” That sin is Jeroboam appointing priests for the high places. It's a heavy way to end the passage, and the text doesn't soften it.

The passage does say it. “…this was the sin of the house of Jeroboam that led to its extermination and destruction from the face of the earth.” The sin is appointing priests for the high places. It's a heavy verse, and it's in the text.
